extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom managers, and journalism stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and prediction about how news organizations should disclose and explain the business side of journalism — funding, salaries, and the editorial/business 'firewall' — to rebuild public trust. Emphasizes practical steps (explainers, public grappling) and examples from nonprofit newsrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share funding information
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsroom managers should disclose how their organizations are funded — revenue streams, major donors, business model mechanics — to help audiences understand why coverage decisions are made. The piece points to nonprofit newsrooms as already being 'especially open' about the relationship between business models and audience approach and recommends for-profit newsrooms follow suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share salary information
rubrics_metrics.description: “journalists will share more about their salaries”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and journalists should be more transparent about pay (e.g., salary ranges or reporting on pay structures) so audiences can appreciate the economic realities of the profession and counter assumptions that individuals are prioritizing profit over public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly grapple with the editorial/business 'firewall'
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees on both sides of the 'firewall' between business and editorial will publicly grapple with the ways they attempt to maintain that firewall and the extent to which it actually exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should openly discuss how they try to keep editorial decisions independent from commercial pressures, where the firewall works, and where it may fail. This includes candid internal-and-public conversations rather than claiming an absolute separation without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain what the 'firewall' means (audience-facing explainer)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A good place to start would be a simple explainer for audiences that guides them through what a 'firewall' even means.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce plain-language, audience-friendly explainers that define the editorial/business firewall, give concrete examples of safeguards and exceptions, and show how decisions are made in practice. The aim is to educate audiences rather than assume they understand newsroom structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about how money influences journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: “We don’t talk about how money influences our journalism,” — the argument that journalists should talk about this will change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly address perceptions and realities of financial influence: acknowledge where revenue incentives shape coverage (e.g., audience-driven story choices) and clarify where they do not. Use evidence and examples to counter simplistic public assumptions (such as 'profits over journalism and over truth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how reporting gets done (process transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: “show people how they go about their reporting, and why their stories come out the way that they do.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase transparency about journalistic methods: sourcing, verification steps, editorial decisions, and resource constraints. This complements business transparency and helps audiences understand both the production and economic contexts of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt nonprofit openness as a model for for-profits
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nonprofit newsrooms have been especially open when it comes to sharing the relationship between their business models and their approach to their audiences. They’re charting a path that for-profit newsrooms will hopefully follow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from nonprofit practices (e.g., public reporting on funding and mission alignment) and adapt them to for-profit contexts where possible. The recommendation is normative: use successful examples as templates for broader industry change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and address public perceptions about profit motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will acknowledge that people’s skepticism toward news is fundamentally tied up in their unflattering misunderstandings about how journalists — and the organizations they work for — make money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively incorporate public sentiment into transparency efforts: recognize that many people assume outlets prioritize audience/profit over truth and make transparency initiatives explicitly aimed at correcting those misunderstandings (e.g., studies of public attitudes cited as motivating evidence).
